The future with will, going to, the present continuous and the present simple in negative form
There are different ways to talk about the present and the future, you can use will or going to to talk about the future and in present you can use the present simple or the present continuous.

In future, you can use will for promises or assumptions related to actions in the future.

This is the structure to form negative statements:

Subject + will not / won't + verb in infinitive without to + complement.

Example:
She won't use C++ after she learns how to use C#.

When you want to talk about plans that are sure or things that you are confident that are happening use going to.

To form negative statements with going to, follow this structure:

Subject + be (am/ is/ are) + not + going to + verb + complement.

Example:
They are not going to use C++

We use the future with going to+ base form for:
• A decision made before the moment of speaking
• A prediction made on evidence (that we see or hear)

If you want to talk about routines in the present, use the present simple. Follow this structure to talk in negative:

Subject + do / does + not + verb in infinitive + complement.
Subject + verb be (am, is, are) + not + complement.

Example:
We don't work with other programming languages.

Had better, ought to, and might want to for what is advisable in negative form
There are certain verbs we can use to show that something is or isn't a good idea, to give advice.
Had better is one of the modal verbs you use to give advice, you use it to say that it's a better idea to do something.
Subject + had better + not + verb ( base form) + complement

Example:

Chris had better not use C to develop desk applications.

You can use ought to in more polite contexts because it's more formal, it is used to give strong suggestions or advice that needs to be followed.

Use the following structure to form negative statements using ought to:
Subject + ought not to + verb ( base form) + complement

Example:
We ought not to use more than two programming languages when developing an app.

Might want to is used to talk about preferences or better options according to the possibilities people may have.

You can use this structure to build negative sentences using might want to:
Subject + might not want to + verb (base form) + complement.
Julian might not want to use that programming language.
But you might not want to give up.
You had better not forget how easy it is to learn how to use it.
You ought not to take this information slightly.

Michael: I'm reading this text about C# because I have an exam tomorrow, but I don't know how to study it.
Melissa: I think that you might not want to memorize everything because you can get confused with some concepts; that happens to me when I try to memorize any text. Instead, let me ask you some questions to know how well you have comprehended the text so that you won't forget anything in your exam.
Michael: Great!

Melissa: So, does C# have any advantage over another programming language?
Michael: Yes. In fact, C# has several benefits; for instance, C# runs programs faster than Java. Plus, its code and its management of events are more legible than C++. In addition, engineers can handle it better because of its comprehensible and standard language.
Melissa: You might not want to forget that it has an automatic collection garbage. This is not as intricate as other programming languages.
Michael: I just need to mention some pros; I'm not going to become an expert overnight.

Melissa: Okay! Let's continue. What is it considered as a myth or truth in C#?
Michael: Some people believe that C# is a Microsoft property, but it's not true. What is a fact is that Microsoft handles some legal rights of C# in the USA so that people use it freely. Moreover, users think that C# runs on Windows only, but this is just a myth. Microsoft has opened a new source called Mono, which runs on other operating systems including Linux server OSes or smartphones OSes. Many users of these operating systems might not want to buy new equipment but with Mono, programmers can build their code on their personal Mac laptops and desktops before running it on the operating system.
Melissa: You ought not to worry, you are not going to fail your exam. Nevertheless, if you have any doubts, you had better ask the teacher before.
Michael: Indeed, I'm booking a session with him later.
